title: The Art of the Fight
subtitle: Field Notes No. 007 · A history of character action
rightsNotice: Game images and quoted material belong to their respective rights holders. Included for commentary and criticism; no endorsement or ownership is implied.
editorial:
Winning a fight and making a fight your own are different pleasures. Character action lives in the gap: the enemy might fall to a safe repeated attack, but the game offers another weapon, a counter, a launch, a dodge that keeps the next move alive. The reward is not only a larger number. It is learning to make decisions faster without reducing them to one answer.

This issue follows that idea from arcade action to the style-driven games associated with Capcom, Team Ninja and PlatinumGames. It is a family history, not a claim that every sword game belongs to one fixed genre. Onimusha still carries survival horror's rooms and puzzles. Blood Will Tell is an action-adventure relative, with an unusually literal model of rebuilding a character. The 2nd Runner puts combat expression into a flying mech. Ghost of Sparta pursues spectacle and pace on a portable system. Their differences matter as much as their resemblance.

Four deep dives cover the PS2 and PSP years: Onimusha, The 2nd Runner, Blood Will Tell and Ghost of Sparta. Devil May Cry 3: Special Edition and Bayonetta get full features too, because a history without their ideas would be missing much of its subject. God Hand already has a deep dive in Field Notes No. 005, so it returns here as part of the lineage rather than a repeated recommendation.

Start with the history for the map, or with The 2nd Runner to see the genre's ideas applied to a flying robot. Each deep dive includes an opening-session plan and the friction that a glowing reputation can hide. This is researched criticism built from manuals, contemporary reviews and developer interviews, not a playtest: no game was launched for this issue, and emulation notes cite upstream project data only. Screenshots, sources and their credits are bundled for offline reading.

articles.deck: Capcom's 2001 samurai game puts a timing-based sword fighter inside a Resident Evil shell of fixed cameras, tank controls, key hunts and mirror saves. The core is a hidden counter-kill called Issen, a soul economy that also opens doors, and a 20-floor Dark Realm, all in a campaign of about five hours.

articles.deck: Kojima produced and Shuyo Murata directed this 2003 sequel, which turns a giant robot into a character-action lead: one attack button that switches between blade and gun by range, dash and burst variants, grabs that make enemies into weapons, and a dozen sub-weapons built around set pieces. This guide covers what the North American disc does and lacks, and what is known (and untested) about emulating it.

articles.deck: Sega and Red Entertainment's 2004 Tezuka adaptation inverts action-game progression: Hyakkimaru starts armed with prosthetic blades and cannons and wins back his real body one fiend at a time. Here's what those parts actually do (mostly stats, with a few famous exceptions), how its arm-blade, gun and Slice combat works, and why its slow start is the catch.

articles.deck: Ready at Dawn squeezed God of War's crowd-control combat, red-orb upgrades and grab finishers onto one analog nub, then added Thera's Bane fire blades and the Arms of Sparta to make up for the missing buttons. A sourced look at the US PSP release, how it differs from Chains of Olympus and the PS2 original, and what upstream PPSSPP data says about emulating it.

articles.deck: Styles, weapon swaps mid-combo, a live style meter and graded missions: Devil May Cry 3 set the rules character action still follows. The 2006 Special Edition is also the one that made its notorious difficulty fair. Here is what changed, how to start, and where it is sold today.
articles.imageCaption: Vergil, playable only in Special Edition, attacks a scythe-wielding demon, with the style meter at "Dope!". PS2 Special Edition, © Capcom, screenshot via GameSpot's 2006 review.

articles.title: Bayonetta: Dodge Late, Keep the Combo
articles.deck: Hideki Kamiya's 2009 reworking of the Devil May Cry template is built on Witch Time, the dodge offset and a medal for every fight. This covers how those systems fit together, why the PS3 port was marked down, and where a God Hand fan may hit friction. Researched from the manual, the official guide and reviews; nothing was playtested.
articles.imageCaption: Gameplay: a demon summoned from Bayonetta's hair mauls a large angel during Verse 4, with the verse number and halo count on screen. © Sega / PlatinumGames. Screenshot supplied with GameSpot's Xbox 360 review (January 2010); capture platform not independently verified.
